To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The expression pattern of the bumblebees’ MRJP-like protein is conserved in the brain, but differs from that of the honeybees’ MRJPs; (2) the expression of MRJPs is restricted to the secretory cells of the hypopharynx, which are located at the base of the hypopharangeal glands; and (3) the expression of the MRJP-like protein of bumblebeess is conserved in their brain

(i) the bumblebee HGs differ significantly from those of the honeybee with respect to morphology, number of cells, and actin organization; (ii) the bumblebees express a single MRJP-like protein (BtRJP), and (iii) BtRJP is expressed in the mushroom bodies and the optic lobes of the brain.

the evolution of a royal jelly protein in the bumblebees, which represents a pre-divergence stage of the royal jelly proteins.
the evolution of MRJPs and the development of HGs, and it provides insights into the evolution of the brain of social insects.

the MRJPs have a dual gland-brains function and that the MRJP gene family evolved in the honeybee to produce royal jelly.

MRJPs are expressed in the brain of bivalve bees and honeybees and that they are expressed in the HGs of the honeybees but not in bivalve bees, which have no HGs.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution of MRJP genes was accompanied by a dramatic shift in the expression of these genes from the brain to the hypopharynx.
the evolution of the honeybee HGs was accompanied by a loss of the gland's dual function, and that this loss is reflected by the loss of BtRJP expression in the bumblebees' HGs.
